title: Seattle's Ballard Light Rail Could Take Until 2060 Without New Funding
excerpt: Sound Transit faces a $7-9 billion gap to extend its Link light rail to Ballard, with the full line potentially delayed decades beyond the 2039 target voters approved in 2016.
body:
• Sound Transit's Ballard Link Extension faces a potential completion date of 2060 if no additional funding is secured, far beyond the voter-approved 2039 target.
  • The agency needs $7-9 billion in new revenue or cost savings to fully fund the 7.7-mile, $20 billion project connecting downtown Seattle to Ballard.
  • Agency leadership insists the project is not cancelled and says it has until 2033 to find full construction funding before being forced to truncate the line at Seattle Center.

Seattle's long-promised light rail extension to the Ballard neighborhood could take until 2060 to complete if Sound Transit fails to close a multi-billion-dollar funding gap, according to estimates based on the agency's own planning data. The timeline represents a stark departure from the 2039 opening date voters approved when they backed the Sound Transit 3 expansion plan in 2016.

The 7.7-mile Ballard Link Extension, which would connect downtown Seattle to the Ballard neighborhood via South Lake Union, Lower Queen Anne, and Interbay, carries a projected cost north of $20 billion. Sound Transit needs an additional $7 to $9 billion in new revenue or cost savings to build the full line, part of a broader $34.5 billion shortfall across the entire ST3 portfolio.

A Project in Limbo

In late May, the Sound Transit board voted to overhaul the ST3 expansion plan, prioritizing the regional light rail "spine" from Tacoma to Everett while deferring stations in Ballard, Interbay, and other Seattle neighborhoods. Under the adopted plan, the line would stop at Seattle Center rather than continuing north to Market Street in Ballard.

"I keep hearing things online or in conversation that are not entirely accurate. The board action to update the system plan did not kill or cancel or delete or defer or postpone the Ballard project."

— Dow Constantine, Sound Transit CEO

Constantine told reporters that $18.1 billion remains committed to Ballard Link, and that the agency would be "aggressively pursuing" options to reduce costs and raise revenue at the federal, state, and local levels. Construction is set to begin in SoDo, with the deep downtown tunnel representing the project's critical path. The agency says it has until 2033 or 2034 to secure full construction funding to build the line as one project, rather than truncating it at Seattle Center.

The Cost of Delay

Former Seattle Department of Transportation director Scott Kubly, who previously led capital financial strategy at Washington's WMATA transit agency, has calculated that Ballard Link could open in the late 2050s under the current deferral trajectory. His estimate assumes construction starting in 2047, at the end of a 20-year window during which Sound Transit says the project is unaffordable, followed by roughly a decade of construction work.

The financial pressure extends beyond the funding gap itself. Brad Owen, Sound Transit's incoming Deputy CEO for Capital Delivery, warned that delays carry real cost escalation. West Seattle Link, a smaller companion project, faces delay costs of $20 to $30 million per month due to inflation. Ballard Link's costs would be even steeper given its larger scale.

Truncating the line at Seattle Center would also cost 34,000 daily boardings, according to agency modeling — more riders than entire planned extensions to Everett (27,100 daily riders) or West Seattle (27,600 daily riders) are expected to attract.

Federal Headwinds

Compounding the challenge, federal transit funding faces potential steep cuts. Sound Transit had been counting on a Federal Transit Administration full funding grant agreement to cover roughly half of West Seattle Link's costs, and federal grants figure into other projects as well. The Trump administration has issued no new transit grants since taking office in 2025 and has attempted to claw back some past awards.

A bipartisan House transportation committee bill would cut programs designed to fund new transit and rail projects by 45%, according to the Urban Institute. If enacted, those cuts could balloon Sound Transit's budget gap further.

Sound Transit is also pursuing longer bond authority through the federal TIFIA loan program after a previous legislative push fell short. Chief Financial Officer Hughey Newsome has described the 75-year bonds as "a tool in a toolkit," though bonding alone appears unlikely to close the full gap.

What's Next

Sound Transit continues environmental review for the full Ballard Link alignment, with a Draft Environmental Impact Statement expected later in 2026. The agency says it will reach 100% design on the full line by 2031, including the unfunded segments, a commitment secured through pressure from Seattle advocates and officials.

Business groups have urged greater transparency. The Ballard Alliance and North Seattle Industrial Association wrote to Sound Transit that "the process feels largely opaque, with insufficient public information available regarding the long-term impacts of near-term decisions."

Meanwhile, alternative proposals have surfaced, including a plan from Kubly and transportation planner Trevor Reed for automated light rail with shorter trains at higher frequencies, modeled after the Copenhagen Metro. Sound Transit has responded with skepticism, citing capacity limitations, though Kubly disputes that assessment.

For Ballard residents who voted for light rail a decade ago, the gap between the 2039 promise and a potential 2060 reality underscores how large infrastructure costs, political priorities, and federal funding uncertainty can reshape even voter-approved transit plans.
